cover.question: Was Mark Twain wrong?
cover.name: TITIAN
cover.answered_by: Twain called it the vilest picture in the world and was sure it was painted for a brothel; the dog (fidelity), the maids with a wedding dress and the myrtle (lasting love) lead many historians to see a marriage painting

facts.claim: Titian, Venus of Urbino, 1538, Uffizi Galleries, Florence; bought from Titian by Guidobaldo II della Rovere (letter of 1538)
Mark Twain, A Tramp Abroad (1880), ch. L: 'the foulest, the vilest, the obscenest picture the world possesses--Titian's Venus'
Twain: 'Without any question it was painted for a bagnio [brothel] and it was probably refused because it was a trifle too strong.'
The sleeping dog at the foot of the bed refers to fidelity in marriage
Behind her, one maid searches a chest (cassone) while the other carries the gold and light-blue wedding dress on her shoulder
The myrtle on the windowsill is linked to Venus and to constant love
Many scholars read it as a marriage painting, possibly for Guidobaldo's marriage to Giulia Varano (1534) or its consummation (hedged)
Guidobaldo called it simply 'the nude woman' (la donna nuda)
It came to Florence with Vittoria della Rovere's dowry (Medici, 1633) and has hung in the Uffizi since 1736

caption:
Mark Twain called this the vilest picture in the world.

In A Tramp Abroad (1880) he described Titian's Venus of Urbino, hanging in the Uffizi's Tribune, as "the foulest, the vilest, the obscenest picture the world possesses". It wasn't her nakedness, he wrote, but "the attitude of one of her arms and hand". And he was sure it had been painted for a bagnio, a brothel.

Now look closer. At her feet a little dog sleeps: for the Uffizi, a sign of fidelity in marriage. Behind her, two maids put away a gold and light-blue wedding dress in a chest. On the windowsill, a myrtle, the plant of Venus and lasting love.

The buyer, Guidobaldo della Rovere, simply called it "the nude woman". Many historians think it was made for a marriage, perhaps his own to Giulia Varano.

P.S. It reached Florence in 1633, in the dowry of Vittoria della Rovere, a bride.

👁️ Who do you believe, Twain or the dog?
